newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK RPI inflation set to edge up in May.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK RPI inflation set to edge up in May.

text.p: A squeeze in seasonal food prices and higher housing costs are likely to produce a rise in May UK headline RPI inflation, but the targeted underlying rate may have stayed steady, analysts said.

A Reuter poll of analysts suggests all-items inflation rose 0.3 percent on the month in May compared with April's 0.6 percent rise, pushing the year-on-year rate up to 2.5 percent from 2.4 percent in April.

But the poll forecasts the targeted measure of RPIX, which excludes volatile mortgage interest payments, stayed steady at 2.5 percent, still bang in line with the government's target rate. The figures are due at 0830 GMT on Thursday.

"Much will depend again on the erratic components such as seasonal food prices," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets. Food prices have been very volatile and falling prices in the seasonal foods category -- down 13.5 percent in the year to April -- have helped keep a lid on overall inflation.

But the Office for National Statistics said at the time of the last release that frost damage to crops in Europe was likely to exert upward pressure on inflation in May, with fruit prices in particular set to rise.

In addition, the quarter point interest rate rise on May 6 triggered mortgage rate rises from most big lenders. But with only new borrowers affected right away, the ONS said the impact would be minimal in May.

Existing borrowers are not due to start paying the higher rates until June, but economists said that after last Friday's rate rise and with several more expected, headline RPI will push ahead of RPIX in the months ahead.

The diverging trend between the prices of goods and services looks set to continue for May, with goods prices expected to stay around April's 1.7 percent year-on-year rate while services prices could nudge up from April's 3.3 percent in response to tighter labour market conditions.

"There is clearly little problem on the goods side, but services prices are rising sharply. The split between the two is largely a sterling issue," said Andrew Snowball, UK economist at the Cooperative Bank.
The strong pound -- up around 18 percent on a trade-weighted basis since last August -- has allowed prices of imported goods to fall sharply.
But the services sector is insulated from this effect and, since it makes up around 40 percent of the total RPI, will continue to exert most of the upward pressure.
"With demand strong and growing stronger this year, that will not go away," said Snowball.
In April, lower rent costs and utilities prices were offset by higher prices for shop and non-shop services. These categories include catering, repairs, domestic services and insurance.
